title: Integrating Language Models and Topology for Multi-Scale R-Loop Prediction
text:
RELEVANCE (See instructions):
R-loops occur commonly in the genome. When improperly regulated by topological stress, they promote
double-strand breaks and chromosomal rearrangements. This research integrates mathematical modeling
and laboratory experiments to define the physical rules of R-loop architecture and predict where and how
these structures form, thus establishing a biophysical foundation to define their role in disease.

title: Confocal Microscope - Leica Stellaris
text:
The Lundquist Institute is requesting funds to acquire a Leica Stellaris FALCON confocal microscope to replace
its aging, 12+-year-old Leica SP8 FLIM confocal system, which has been heavily used for imaging in both live
and fixed tissues. Acquiring this advanced instrument is key to sustaining and enhancing the work of a highly
active group of NIH-funded investigators. The new system will support cutting-edge research in areas such
as cancer, diabetes, genetic disorders, development and stem cell research, host/pathogen interaction and
mechanisms of immunity, metabolic disorders, DNA damage, neuroimmune and neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Digital Biomarkers of Post-traumatic Osteoarthritis: Toward Precision Rehabilitation
text:
Every year, nearly 400,000 Americans rupture their anterior cruciate ligament and more than half of them
develop post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA) within 15 years. By objectively capturing movement during both
natural environment ambulation and physical therapy, the proposed research will inform the development of
more effective rehabilitation therapies assisted by wearable technology and computer vision/machine learning,
promising to halt PTOA and extend the lifespan of natural joints.

title: Determining the mechanisms of Toxoplasma gondii colonization and crossing of the placental barrier
text:
We still have limited knowledge about how some pathogens, such as the eukaryotic parasite Toxoplasma
gondii (T. gondii), are vertically transmitted from the mother, causing fetal malformations and death worldwide.
We use a new in vitro placental barrier and pregnant guinea pig models to describe the role of T. gondii protein
TgMIF in vertical transmission and aim to identify novel parasitic effectors enhancing T. gondii's capacity to
cross the placental barrier. These discoveries will offer insights into the mechanistic aspects of T. gondii vertical
transmission and potentially lead to the development of new therapeutics protecting the fetus from infections.

title: PATCHES - Physiological Assessment Technology for Child-Caregiver Health and Emotional Synchrony
text:
This study will validate a phone-linked chest patch and companion app that capture caregivers’ and young
autistic children’s heart signals, synchronized video of their shared activities, and brief on-the-spot surveys in
everyday home settings. By demonstrating that the platform can accurately monitor caregiver-child physiological
synchrony, this novel platform will lay the foundation for future studies aiming to personalize and optimize
caregiver support and parent-mediated interventions, ultimately improving both caregiver mental health and child
developmental trajectories.

title: TBEL Project 3
text: PROJECT 3 - ABSTRACT Pancreatic cancer arises from non-invasive precursor lesions that are curable if detected and treated early. Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) is the most common of these precursor lesions and represents a critical target of early detection and cancer prevention approaches. Previous studies from our group have highlighted critical genomic alterations that drive clonal expansion and neoplastic progression in some PanINs. These studies have also demonstrated that expansion and progression can occur without the accumulation of additional driver genomic alterations, suggesting that diverse driver mechanisms operate in different PanINs. The overall hypothesis of this proposal is that the transition to HG PanIN can be driven by genomic or precursor microenvironment (PME) alterations, with distinct drivers dominating in different lesions. To investigate this hypothesis, the proposed studies will evaluate both cell intrinsic and cell extrinsic drivers of neoplastic progression in human PanIN samples. We will employ a novel approach that allows both three-dimensional reconstruction and molecular analysis of human PanIN samples. We will perform multi-region whole exome sequencing and evolutionary reconstruction in order to correlate genomic alterations with expansion and progression of neoplastic cells in three dimensions. In order to identify non-genetic drivers of neoplastic progression, we will analyze immune and stromal cell subsets in the same three-dimensionally reconstructed PanIN samples using imaging mass cytometry, allowing us to determine the variability of key components of the PME across multiple regions of these PanIN samples. This complementary analysis will allow us to correlate the microenvironmental features with the molecular alterations in associated PanIN cells. We will also integrate predicted neoantigens and T-cell receptor sequencing on the same PanIN regions, providing a multi-dimensional analysis of the immune response to PanINs. Taken together, these approaches will systematically evaluate potential drivers of progression in the neoplastic cells and associated immune response, providing crucial biological insights and a rational foundation for novel early detection and prevention approaches.

title: Validating Artificial Intelligence Based Surgical Skill Assessment for Robotic Hiatal Hernia Repair Using A Deep Learning Vision Transformer Model
text:
Surgical skill is a key determinant of patient outcomes, yet current methods for assessing intraoperative
performance remain subjective and difficult to scale. This project will harness artificial intelligence and
computer vision to develop an automated, objective tool for evaluating surgical skill, laying the foundation for
future investigations into the relationship between surgical skills and patient outcomes and contributing to the
development of AI-driven feedback systems. By advancing AI-driven surgical assessment, this work
contributes to a broader goal of enhancing surgical training and healthcare quality in minimally invasive and
robotic surgery.

title: Integrating Multi-Trait Genetics, Proteomics, and Deep Learning to Uncover Biomarkers and Therapeutic Targets for COPD Exacerbations
text:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a serious and common lung disease that causes frequent
breathing flare-ups, hospitalizations, and early death. This project will combine genetic data, proteins in
people's blood, and artificial intelligence models built from COPD lung cell data to better predict who is most at
risk for these flare-ups and to understand the molecular reasons behind their increased risk. The ultimate goal
of this project is to guide new strategies to prevent these episodes and improve care for people living with
COPD.

title: Elucidation of a post-transcriptional regulatory node in macrophage function
text:
Our work, which requires the development of a new chemical proteomics platform, explores how proteins
acquired at the surface of macrophage/monocytes during cell-cell interactions can initiate protein-level changes
that result in a new macrophage state. This work will reveal how new immune cell types arise and may inform
the development of macrophage-targeting therapeutics in disease contexts.

title: Improving diagnosis of post-traumatic sepsis using plasma microbial DNA sequencing
text:
Sepsis is a life-threatening emergency that requires rapid diagnosis of infections and treatment with antibiotics.
In trauma patients, diagnosis of sepsis is particularly challenging because initial injury itself can cause
physiological derangements that mimic those attributed to infections. In this project, we propose to develop
biomarkers to improve diagnostics, clinical management, and outcomes for sepsis in trauma patients using
sequencing analysis of circulating microbial DNA in plasma.

title: Exploring the contribution of extracellular vesicles to epileptogenesis in TLE and DS
text:
In this exploratory R21 proposal, we will test the hypothesis that alterations in the properties of brain derived
extracellular vesicles (BDEVs), which are small particles that are released by cells in the brain, contribute to the
development of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE) and Dravet syndrome (DS). The data generated by these
experiments will provide new insight into the role of BDEVs in the pathogenesis of MTLE and DS, and might
potentially identify novel targets for therapeutic intervention.

title: Optimization of structure-guided models of peptide presentation and T-cell receptor specificity
text:
Current cancer immunotherapies, such as checkpoint blockade, succeed in treating only a minority of patients,
revealing a critical public health problem rooted in the inability to precisely match T-cell receptors (TCRs) to the
specific mutation-derived neoantigens they recognize. The Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) is central
to this process, as it displays processed peptide antigens, making them visible to the T cells, and thus accurate
prediction of both MHC presentation and subsequent TCR binding is the key bottleneck to creating precise
therapies. This project addresses this challenge by developing highly accurate AI models to reliably predict these
necessary TCR-antigen pairs and MHC presentation, enabling the design of personalized cancer
immunotherapies and improved disease monitoring.

title: Mixed methods examination of warning signs within 24 hours of suicide attempt in hospitalized adults
text:
Warning signs signal immediate risk for suicidal behavior and their assessment is of critical importance in
acute care settings including emergency departments and crisis lines. This innovative 4-year study analyzes
adult hospital patients’ stories of their suicide attempts in their own words and through systematic review of the
hours leading up to the attempt. The project is designed to discover warning signs that have been overlooked,
to clarify which warning signs confer especially high risk, and to explore the language patients use to describe
warning signs, results that are critical to improve risk assessment in acute care settings.

title: Immunogenics and Flow Cytometry
text: IMMUNOGEONOMICS AND FLOW CYTOMETRY SHARED RESOURCE The Immunogenomics and Flow Cytometry SR (IMCF) is a hybrid core that provides access to state-of-the-art techniques such as mass cytometry and immunogenomics analysis of bulk and single cell next generation sequencing data coupled with a high utilization Flow Cytometry facility with a 30-year LCCC history. New immune monitoring capabilities were developed in response to investigator needs, particularly for the analysis of immune responses in preclinical tumor models and human clinical research. The immunogenomics component offers a full suite of immunogenomics techniques, including immune gene signature and pathway analysis, cell phenotype deconvolution, MHC haplotype prediction, neoantigen prediction, T cell and B cell repertoire profiling, and systems level analyses such as cytokine network analysis and integrated survival modeling. This is joined by an investment in CyTOF for expanded panel analysis of cellular phenotypes. This component currently supports correlative science for tissues being collected from eight immunotherapy trials and multiple in vivo animal models of cancer. In addition to these new capabilities, the facility also houses a full complement of highly used analytic flow cytometers and cell sorters for both mouse and human work, New purchases in addition the CyTOF are two new spectral analytic machines. Most important for the research community, all SR components have expert staff to support investigators in experimental design, sample processing, data acquisition, and downstream analysis. IMCF is led by Dr. Vincent, MD, an expert in immunogenomics and Dr. Fisher, PhD who has led the LCC Flow facility since 2010 and has over 30 years’ experience in flow cytometry. The budget requested ($211,126) is a small proportion of the total operating budget of $1.7M. Flow cytometry is a traditionally heavily used facility; 80 members were users in fiscal year 2019.

title: Project 2: Immune Response Analysis
text: The purpose of this Project is to apply advanced multi-omics techniques to comprehensively analyze humoral immune responses to promising HIV vaccine immunogens. Our mission is to advance vaccine development by extracting as much information as possible from each immunization trial to best inform the optimal design, composition and delivery of a cohesive immunogen matrix that reliably induces broad, protective HIV immunity. We have devised three Specific Aims which outline the steps necessary to accomplish these goals. Successful completion of these Aims will require indispensable contributions from every component of the MOVE Consortium. In Aim 1, we will deeply characterize the immune response to priming immunogens designed to activate bnAb precursors of one or more specificities (Project 1). While many aspects of this Aim are designed to evaluate the extent to which immunogens are working as designed, equally important is identifying specific genetic and structural features which need improvement during subsequent rounds of refinement and re- evaluation (Structural Proteomics Core). In Aim 2, we will evaluate the human immunogenicity of candidate priming immunogens by isolating immunogen-specific mAbs from HIV-naive humans. This is a critically important aspect of our vaccine development process, as these mAbs are most accurate representation, short of a human clinical trial, of the humoral immune response that will be triggered in actual human vaccine recipients. These mAbs will also be used to create humanized animal models for more thorough vaccine evaluation (Animal Models Core). In Aim 3, we will use our single cell immune multi-omics platform to rapidly evaluate the immune response to sequential vaccine immunogens in near real-time, using the resulting B cell profiles of specificity and function to inform selection of optimal candidates for subsequent boosts. Seamless data sharing between MOVE components and sophisticated tools for visualization and analysis (Data Management & Bioinformatics Core) will allow these analyses to occur within the normal time interval between sequential immunizations. We can then dynamically adjust the parameters of each immunization experiment to maximize our likelihood of success by focusing our experimental resources on the most promising immunogen designs.

title: Dissecting the molecular mechanism of the cardiac fight-or-flight response via real-time light-controlled phosphorylation of Rad
text:
Medications targeting upstream factors in the cardiac fight-or-flight response are vital for treating heart failure,
arrhythmias, and ischemic heart disease, but their lack of cardiac specificity often leads to undesirable side
effects. This research aims to uncover how phosphorylation of Rad, a key downstream regulator of this
response in the heart, controls calcium channel function. By identifying novel pathways for cardiac-specific
drug development, this study has the potential to improve treatments for cardiovascular disease and enhance
public health outcomes.

title: Computational methods for sub-cellular spatial transcriptomics with high gene coverage
text:
We propose to develop innovative computational methods and bioinformatics toolkits for spatial transcriptomics
data from new technologies. Our proposed models will address challenges interpreting large data sets
accurately and provide fundamental understanding of the difference between cell types in various tissues.
Discoveries of how cells are spatially organized will link tissue and disease biology to precision medicine and
human health.

title: ADAPT: Autonomous Delirium Monitoring and Adaptive Prevention
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it can result in enhanced critical care workflow and
early critical care intervention, ultimately improving patient outcomes and decreasing hospitalization costs.
Thus, the proposed research is relevant to the part of NIH's mission that pertains to advancing disease
diagnosis through medical applications of new tools and technologies, as the proposed research applies
advanced computational methods and sensing technologies to automatically quantify and convey patient
status in real-time.

title: Targeting the longevity regulator PAPP-A with small molecule inhibitors
text:
The proposed work will generate first-in-class small molecule inhibitors of the PAPP-A protease, which
will be useful chemical tools to explore the biology of IGF1 signaling, and serve as promising candidate
anti-aging compounds. Mice lacking PAPP-A show extended lifespan and protection from diverse age-
associated diseases. The proposed work is therefore relevant to NIA’s mission to support biological
research on aging, and to NIH’s larger mission to foster research to protect and improve health.

title: Mitochondrial transport and quality control in neurons
text:
Relevance
Many neurodegenerative diseases increase prevalence in aging population and affect
mitochondrial functions. An effective treatment is desperately needed but the underlying
molecular and cellular mechanisms of their destructive path remain poorly understood. This
proposal aims to understand mechanisms underlying mitochondrial quality control and
movement in neurons, impaired in multiple diseases, and is therefore relevant to public health
and the mission of the NIH.
